title: Argentine national women’s team soccer coach accused of sexual abuse by former players | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

As far back as she can remember, soccer player Florencia Mercau has supported one of Argentina’s best-known teams – River Plate. So when in 2014 the call came telling her she would be moving to Buenos Aires to join the club of her childhood heroes, Mercau was over the moon.

For a young girl who grew up in a poor neighbourhood of Marquesado, in San Juan province, “it was the best thing I’ve ever been told,” Mercau said. “I’m a River fan. The chance to be at (Argentina’s) biggest club, and to know that, after the tough childhood I had, that I was able to reach River… It was my dream and I’ll give it my all.”

But that dream quickly began to unravel, she said, when a week after she joined, age 20, she met the club’s recently hired new coach, Diego Guacci.

“Not even a day had gone by and he sent me a text, addressing me as ‘Flor’ and saying, ‘Could you send me some nude photos,’” Mercau told CNN in an exclusive interview, the first time she has publicly discussed the abuse she says she endured.

She says she deleted the texts and fought off Guacci’s advances, but that only provoked what she felt was a more dangerous version of him.

“He’d come to me in practice and grab me from behind… he’d tell me, ‘delete the conversation, delete it because if you don’t, I will kill you and all your family,’” she said. “I didn’t even want to tell my mom because I thought it was wrong – I thought I was the one who was wrong.”

Traumatized by the abuse, she said, but still wanting to play for the team she loved, Mercau found herself in an impossible position. One day, she said, she felt she could no longer continue.

“In that moment I made the worst decision, I said I don’t want to live anymore, I don’t want to endure it anymore,” she said. “I don’t want to suffer anymore; I don’t deserve it because I always gave my best.”

Mercau, now 32, survived the suicide attempt and is one of five Argentinian footballers to recently file a complaint with FIFA, soccer’s international governing body, against Diego Guacci. They accuse the former River Plate and Argentinian women’s national youth team coach of inappropriate conduct, including sexual harassment, threats and psychological abuse.

But this isn’t the first time FIFA has been alerted to his alleged abuse.

In 2020 and 2021, five other women filed a complaint alleging sexual harassment and psychological abuse, and even testified in an official FIFA investigation into Guacci. An investigatory committee recommended sanctioning him in 2021, but Guacci – who has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing – emerged from the ordeal mostly unscathed.

“The Chamber believes that the evidence on file is insufficient to corroborate, to its comfortable satisfaction, the Players’ account of the events,” the adjudicatory chamber of FIFA’s Ethics Committee said in its findings.

“Notwithstanding the above, the Chamber wished to stress that such conclusion shall not be considered as a recognition that the reported facts did not occur.”

The decision left Guacci, who had moved on from River Plate to coach U15 and U17 women at the Argentinian national team, free to continue coaching, and the players in shock.

It was “an absolute blow,” one of the players who filed the initial complaint, Gabriela Garton, told CNN. “If five players’ testimony is not enough, what do you need?”

The new complaint has now fed into a political firestorm in Argentina, after Guacci’s wife, Andrea Guacci, brought further attention to the case by helping draft legislation that would increase jail time for those convicted of falsely accusing someone of a crime involving gender violence, sexual abuse, or crimes against minors.

Critics say the legislation, which is expected to be voted on soon in the senate, is an alarming attempt to erode hard-won protections for women under a right-wing government which critics say has shown little concern for gender-based violence.

Diego Guacci declined CNN’s request for an interview and did not respond to questions regarding the allegations against him, which he denies.

Garton, a former Argentinian national team player, was one of the first to file a complaint about Guacci’s behaviour, six years ago. Garton was 23 when she began playing for River Plate and had been at the club for a year when Guacci joined in 2014. Initially she had been excited to work with him, saying he seemed “really enthusiastic about women’s football” and appeared to want to “push the game forward.”

But then Garton says the red flags started appearing. First, three or four players who’d worked with him before left the club, saying they “didn’t want to work with him,” she said.

Months later she found out why.

One of her teammates told her that Guacci had exposed himself to her, sending nude photos – and asking for nudes in return – and that player’s testimony was also part of the original FIFA investigation against Guacci.

After that, Garton says she began to notice Guacci’s coercive behavior. One instance, after a difficult loss to rivals Boca Juniors, was so vile she still remembers it vividly, she said.

“After the game, he said something along the lines of like, ‘if you girls play like that again, I’m going to put you all in the showers and… f**k you in the ass,’” Garton recalled.

She too began thinking about leaving the club, while at the same time focusing on her call-up to the Argentinian women’s national team. That didn’t sit well with Guacci, she said.

“He was saying that my behaviour was quite despicable, and that at the end of the day, I was like everyone else on the national team, willing to pull down my pants and be raped to be on the national team,” Garton said.

Garton’s testimony became part of a FIFA investigation process that lasted roughly two years after soccer’s ruling body was first made aware of the allegations against Guacci in January 2020 and began a preliminary probe.

FIFPRO, a global organization that represents professional soccer players, became involved the following month. By November 2020, FIFPRO had provided FIFA with a full report on behalf of four players, acting as legal representative for them. A fifth player came forward in 2021.

“The investigation was almost non-existent. The procedure was extremely slow and sloppy,” FIFPRO’s senior legal counsel Alexandra Gómez Bruinewoud told CNN.

FIFA launched formal investigation proceedings in April 2021 and invited Guacci to respond. In September of that year, he submitted a nine-page statement rejecting the accusations.

Despite his rebuttal, the investigatory chamber found him to have breached several articles of FIFA’s Code of Ethics. It concluded that he sexually harassed one of the players and psychologically abused the others, recommending to the adjudicatory chamber that he be sanctioned.

But that never happened. Soon afterwards, the three-man adjudicatory panel concluded there wasn’t enough evidence to impose any sort of sanction.

“How many players need to present their testimony for a panel – a panel composed only of men – to decide that there was abuse?” Gómez Bruinewoud said.

Guacci and his supporters, chief among them his wife Andrea, have publicly spun the outcome as an acquittal and launched a PR and legal campaign against the accusers, filing lawsuits against the five players and one journalist that became involved in the story. The same players and said journalist have also filed counter defamation claims against Guacci and those cases are still ongoing in Argentina.

“It’s all lies, all lies,” Guacci repeatedly alleged in interviews on Argentinian television and social media segments, claiming the five players didn’t have the courage to show up for his hearing.

“We were never invited to the hearing with the adjudicatory chamber,” Gómez Bruinewoud countered. “We found out there was a hearing with Guacci after it happened.”

Adding to the players’ distress, Guacci also publicly named four of the women he believed were accusing him during the investigation. The players’ lawyers say FIFA then compounded the violation by publishing their initials in its final report, making their identification much easier.

The outed players felt they had little choice but to publicly defend themselves in the face of a brutal smear campaign, which saw them attacked on social media by the Guaccis and their allies. The players and those who spoke out on their behalf say they were pressured and even threatened by Guacci’s supporters in a bid to make them walk back their accusations.

Despite the pressure, Gabriela Garton, Luana Muñoz, Aldana Cometti and Camila Gómez Ares have maintained their version of events – the fifth player, known only as player E, has too, but decided to remain anonymous.

CNN asked FIFA about the initial accusations against Guacci, and the fresh allegations put forward this year.

Soccer’s governing body did not respond to questions sent by CNN, but defended its ruling and the procedures it has in place, saying it takes “any allegation of misconduct reported to it, including sexual abuse and harassment, extremely seriously and has a clear process in place.” It added that investigations follow the principle of due process, in accordance with its own code of ethics, guided by the law in Switzerland – where it is based – the European Court of Human Rights and the Court of Arbitration for Sport.

FIFA also did not confirm or deny it was looking into fresh allegations against Guacci, though insiders have told CNN it is normal for the organization not to disclose whether or not it has opened an investigation.

Although FIFA didn’t sanction Guacci, the Argentine Football Association (AFA) decided not to renew his contract. Guacci and his wife say the accusations against him destroyed his career and he has since moved to Italy.

CNN was able to trace Guacci to a small town in central Italy. Two social media announcements from FC Fossacesia indicate he has been working with a youth team since July.

The club confirmed Guacci had been volunteering with the team but provided no additional details.

CNN reached out to Guacci and exchanged several emails with the former River Plate and Argentina manager over more than a month, submitting multiple requests for an interview.

In his responses, Guacci repeatedly denied the allegations but declined to sit down for an interview or to answer any questions.

Guacci claimed ongoing defamation lawsuits in Argentina prevented him from speaking publicly.

Guacci has said in media appearances that he would like to resume his coaching career in Argentina, where the political climate has shifted under the right-wing government of President Javier Milei.

Andrea Guacci has been a vocal advocate of the draft bill that would increase penalties for making false accusations of violence, proposed in 2024. She has presented her husband’s case as an example of a life forever damaged by what the couple say were false allegations against him.

In Argentina, false accusations of gender-based violence account for a tiny fraction of complaints, according to a 2026 study by Argentina’s public prosecutor’s office.

Andrea Guacci did not respond to CNN’s requests for comment.

For Luana Muñoz, one of the five athletes who first filed the complaint against Guacci, the fact FIFA’s controversial decision is now being used by Andrea Guacci to promote this agenda is particularly worrying.

“We started this to protect women, to protect kids, and it’s concerning because it will mean that they will take rights away from women,” Muñoz told CNN of the proposed bill, adding that it could make it even more difficult for victims of abuse to come forward.

Both Muñoz and Garton said they were hopeful that with five more women coming forward in the new complaint against Guacci, soccer’s governing body would reopen the case.

“You see women’s football and women’s rights in the world, how far we’ve come, but when things like this happen they kind of make you put your feet on the ground and understand there’s so much more that we have to fight for,” Muñoz said.

Mercau has stayed out of the spotlight since her suicide attempt. But she told CNN that she too was committed to pursuing the case despite fears of retribution.

“I’m scared to walk, I’m even scared to breathe,” she said. “But it’s that fear that won’t let me rest; that’s why I’m here today – so that all this can come to an end and I can get on with my life in peace.”

Sol Amaya contributed reporting from Buenos Aires.

Sol Amaya contributed reporting from Buenos Aires.
